reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Results from occlusion of the rostral (apical) basilar artery, usually embolic, causing ischaemia of the midbrain, thalamus, and occipitotemporal lobes
Produces a striking combination of visual, oculomotor, behavioural, and consciousness disturbances rather than prominent limb weakness
Vertical gaze palsy, convergence abnormalities, and pupillary changes reflect involvement of the rostral midbrain and pretectal region
Somnolence, hypersomnolence, or fluctuating consciousness follows bilateral paramedian thalamic and reticular involvement
Cortical visual loss, visual hallucinations (peduncular hallucinosis), and memory disturbance arise from occipitotemporal and thalamic infarction
Motor deficits may be minimal, so the diagnosis is easily missed if attention focuses only on limb power
It is a neurological emergency because it often reflects distal basilar embolism amenable to recanalisation
reference.pathophysiology: Top-of-the-basilar syndrome follows occlusion, typically embolic, of the distal basilar artery and its terminal branches, which supply the midbrain, thalamus, and the medial temporal and occipital lobes through the posterior cerebral and thalamoperforating arteries. Ischaemia of the rostral midbrain and pretectum disrupts vertical gaze, convergence, and pupillary control, while bilateral paramedian thalamic and reticular infarction impairs arousal and produces somnolence and behavioural change. Involvement of the occipitotemporal cortex causes cortical visual loss, visual hallucinations, and amnesia. The clustering of eye movement, arousal, visual, and memory deficits with relatively preserved strength reflects this rostral posterior-circulation territory.
additionalDifferentials: Bilateral paramedian thalamic infarction from an artery of Percheron occlusion
Basilar migraine or other transient posterior circulation events
additionalInvestigations: Diffusion-weighted MRI showing infarction across midbrain, thalamus, and occipitotemporal regions
CT or MR angiography of the basilar apex and posterior circulation to identify occlusion
Urgent vascular imaging to assess suitability for thrombolysis or thrombectomy
Assessment of vertical gaze, pupils, and level of consciousness
Cardiac evaluation for an embolic source including ECG and echocardiography
Thiamine status and metabolic screen where an encephalopathic mimic is possible
redFlags: Fluctuating or declining consciousness signalling active basilar apex occlusion
Progressive brainstem signs indicating evolving basilar thrombosis needing urgent intervention
Bilateral thalamic involvement causing profound hypersomnolence
Cortical blindness with denial of deficit that may mask serious infarction
reference.prognosis: Outcome hinges on the extent of infarction and speed of recanalisation; timely reperfusion can yield good recovery, but extensive rostral brainstem and bilateral thalamic infarction carries high morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Attributing somnolence and confusion to a metabolic cause and missing basilar occlusion
Focusing on limb power and overlooking the diagnostic eye movement and visual signs
Delaying vascular imaging in a patient without obvious hemiparesis
Mistaking peduncular hallucinosis for a primary psychiatric disturbance
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
